problem:
Which of the following statements are true? 

- If $A$ is *any* matrix, then $A{A}^{T}$ is always symmetric.
- The sum of two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is always symmetric.
- The product of two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is always symmetric.

examples.knowledge_point: Identifying True Statements Regarding Properties of Symmetric Matrices
examples.problem:
Which of the following statements are true?

- If $A$ is *any* $n\times n$ matrix, then $A+A^T$ is always symmetric.

- The difference between two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is symmetric.

- The product of two $n\times n$ symmetric matrices is symmetric.
examples.worked_solution:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A = A^T
$$

Equivalently, $a_{ij} = a_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal.

With that in mind, let's examine our statements in turn.

- Statement I is true. Indeed, for any matrix $A,$ we have 

$$
\begin{aligned}(A+{A}^{T})^{T} & ={A}^{T}+({A}^{T})^{T} \\  & ={A}^{T}+A \\  & =A+{A}^{T}.\end{aligned}
$$

- Statement II is true. Indeed, the sum or difference between two symmetric matrices is symmetric.

- Statement III is false. As a counterexample, consider the symmetric matrices 
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture-workers/linear/14050120/assets/f8d153708f7872d0c96414a77c12379d40c6b60a5f08844945fb8a8f8c1809ab.png)
Their product is not symmetric:

$$
\begin{aligned}AB & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & 0\end{aligned}][\begin{aligned}0 & 1 \\ 1 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "I and II only."

feedback.problem:
Which of the following matrices are symmetric?

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}],\,Q=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}],\,R=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$
feedback.worked_solution:
A square matrix $A$ is symmetric if it is equal to its transpose:

$$
A={A}^{T}
$$

Equivalently, ${a}_{ij}={a}_{ji}$ for all $i,j.$ In other words, $A$ is symmetric across its main diagonal. 

With that in mind, let's examine each matrix in turn.

- $P$ is *not* a symmetric matrix. Since ${p}_{13}\ne {p}_{31},$ we obtain $P\ne {P}^{T}.$

$$
P=[\begin{aligned}0 & 1 & 2 \\ 1 & 0 & -1 \\ -1 & 2 & 0\end{aligned}]
$$

- $Q$ is *not* a symmetric matrix. Since ${q}_{13}\ne {q}_{31},$ we obtain $Q\ne {Q}^{T}.$

$$
Q=[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 & -1 \\ 0 & 0 & \sqrt{2} \\ 1 & 2 & -1\end{aligned}]
$$

- $R$ is *not* a symmetric matrix. Since ${r}_{12}\ne {r}_{21},$ we obtain $R\ne {R}^{T}.$

$$
R=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1 & 0 \\ -1 & 0 & 1\end{aligned}]
$$

Therefore, the correct answer is "None of the matrices are symmetric."
